paper_title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.

sections.content: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation Haocheng Wang1,3, Youquan Liu1, Weiyu Guo2, Aokai Zhang3, Donghang Wu4, Hongyu Liu5, Sha Zhang2, Weidong Yang1, Ben Fei2 Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields SR = 0 despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera L2 and Gaussian blur L1 both yield SR = 0.188, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0% and 36.4%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as multi-dimensional property of execution rather than single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift. I. INTRODUCTION Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an increasingly important paradigm for robotic manipulation by integrating visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions within unified policy frameworks [1], [2]. Despite their growing capabilities, maintaining reliable behavior under distribution shifts remains key challenge for deployment, as robots may encounter variations in observations, environments, and physical states that differ from those seen during training. Systematically evaluating VLA robustness under such distribution shifts is important for understanding the reliability of these models in robotic applications. Recent robustness benchmarks have expanded the evaluation of VLA policies beyond nominal task settings through diverse controlled distribution shifts and increasingly systematic evaluation protocols [3][5]. Despite this broader coverage, robustness is still commonly summarized at the task or 1 Fudan University. 2 The Chinese University of Hong Kong. 3 Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, Shenzhen, China. 4 University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. 5 Shanghai Jiao Tong University. evaluation-condition level through aggregate metrics such as success rate. Such summaries do not reveal how individual executions change under distribution shift or where failures emerge within long-horizon task execution, leaving need for more diagnostic evaluation at the execution level. Such diagnosis requires controlling episode-level variation for meaningful comparison, since clean and shifted evaluations with different task instances or initial conditions may confound episode difficulty with the target distribution shift. We therefore compare each perturbed execution with corresponding clean execution under the same underlying task conditions, changing only the target perturbation. This counterfactual pairing provides controlled basis for identifying episode-level outcome changes associated with the evaluated shift. Even under such controlled comparisons, binary task outcome provides only coarse description of failure in longhorizon manipulation. These tasks unfold through sequence of semantically meaningful subgoals [6], [7], so two failed executions may terminate after very different amounts of task progress. Stage-aware evaluation can therefore complement final success or failure by tracking semantic progress and identifying the first incomplete subgoal, providing clearer view of where robustness failures emerge during execution. We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 [3] for evaluating VLA policies under controlled distribution shifts in long-horizon household manipulation, as illustrated in Figure 1. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor shifts at multiple frozen severity levels and matched clean-perturbed protocol for episode-level counterfactual comparison. It further incorporates simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics to track semantic execution progress and localize where failures emerge during long-horizon task execution. RoboCasa-Shift characterizes robustness from complementary perspectives, including end-to-end task outcomes, episode-level outcome changes, and stage-aware execution behavior. Our evaluation reveals that robustness responses vary across perturbation factors and tasks, and that increasing calibrated severity does not always lead to monotonic degradation in end-to-end performance. Aggregate success rates can also mask considerable episode-level outcome changes, while similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to failures emerging at different semantic depths of task execution. Stage-aware analysis further shows that perturbation severity Fig. 1: Overview of RoboCasa-Shift. RoboCasa-Shift evaluates VLA robustness on selected long-horizon RoboCasa tasks under controlled single-factor distribution shifts with multiple frozen severity levels. Strictly matched clean-perturbed rollouts enable counterfactual comparison under shared task conditions, while robustness is characterized jointly through end-to-end task outcomes and stage-aware semantic execution diagnostics. Representative findings illustrate that aggregate success rates can mask substantial episode-level outcome changes, similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to different failure locations, and severe visual corruption can shift failures toward earlier stages of task execution. can alter the semantic depth reached by failed executions, with stronger shifts in some conditions associated with earlier incomplete milestones. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We develop RoboCasa-Shift, diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 for long-horizon household manipulation. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor distribution shifts at multiple frozen severity levels under an episode-level clean-perturbed counterfactual protocol, enabling robustness changes to be examined under matched task conditions. We introduce simulator-grounded stage-aware robustness diagnostic that complements final task success with semantic execution information. Long-horizon tasks are represented through ordered semantic subgoals evaluated by simulator-state predicates, allowing execution progress and the first incomplete subgoal to be tracked for failure localization. We conduct controlled robustness study on four clean-qualified long-horizon RoboCasa tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, jointly analyzing end-to-end task outcomes, counterfactual episode-level changes, and stage-aware execution depth. The analysis reveals robustness behaviors not captured by aggregate success alone, including heterogeneous severity responses and differences in the semantic depth reached by failed executions. II. RELATED WORK A. Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Manipulation VLA models have emerged as promising paradigm for robot manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction within unified policy framework [1], [2]. Building on large-scale and heterogeneous robot datasets, subsequent works have further developed generalist policies that can operate across diverse tasks, robot embodiments, and observation or action spaces [8], [9]. Recent studies have continued to extend VLA models toward more complex sequential manipulation by improving temporal reasoning and visual grounding during task execution [10], [11]. As VLA policies expand to diverse and complex manipulation settings, evaluating their reliability under distribution shifts becomes increasingly important. B. Robustness and Generalization Benchmarks for Robot Manipulation Existing robot manipulation benchmarks have increasingly emphasized generalization beyond the training distribution by evaluating policies across diverse tasks, environments, and controlled variations [12], [13]. More recent benchmarks have substantially expanded this direction by evaluating generalist robot policies under increasingly diverse and systematically controlled distribution shifts [3] [5]. These benchmarks support systematic analysis across perturbation factors, difficulty levels, and task variations, providing broad measurements of policy robustness and generalization. However, such analyses predominantly characterize performance at the task or evaluation-condition level, providing limited information about how distribution shifts affect the semantic execution process within long-horizon task. RoboCasa-Shift complements these efforts through controlled distribution-shift evaluation, episode-level counterfactual comparison, and semantic subgoal-aware diagnosis of robustness degradation in long-horizon execution. C. Long-Horizon and Compositional Manipulation Evaluation Recent progress in robot manipulation evaluation has extended benchmark tasks from short-horizon skills to longhorizon and multi-stage executions that require policies to coordinate multiple interactions over time [14][16]. Beyond increasing task horizon, several benchmarks further expose the temporal or subtask structure of manipulation tasks to evaluate capabilities such as planning, sequential reasoning, and memory-dependent execution [6], [7]. Despite these advances, such task structure is primarily used to characterize long-horizon manipulation capabilities themselves, while its role as diagnostic unit for robustness under controlled distribution shifts remains less explored. RoboCasa-Shift builds on this structured view of long-horizon execution by using semantic subgoals to track execution progress and characterize the semantic depth under distribution shifts. III. ROBOCASA-SHIFT BENCHMARK Figure 2 summarizes the overall evaluation pipeline. RoboCasa-Shift defines diagnostic robustness evaluation protocol for long-horizon household manipulation. It combines clean-competence task screening, controlled singlefactor shifts with frozen severity levels, and matched cleanFig. 2: Pipeline of RoboCasa-Shift. (a) Task Suite. Candidate RoboCasa tasks are filtered through clean-competence screening to construct the formal evaluation suite. (b) Controlled Shifts. Selected tasks are evaluated under four singlefactor distribution shifts with calibrated and frozen severity levels. (c) Counterfactual Pairing. Clean and perturbed rollouts share the underlying task conditions and policy seed and differ only in the target shift. (d) Diagnosis. RoboCasas official task outcome is complemented by stage-aware semantic diagnostics of execution progress, first incomplete subgoal, and subgoal reach. perturbed counterfactual rollouts. RoboCasas official tasksuccess criterion is retained for end-to-end evaluation, while semantic subgoals tracked through simulator-state predicates provide complementary stage-aware diagnostics of execution progress. The formal study in this paper instantiates this protocol on the clean-qualified task suite described below. A. Task Suite We screen 16 pre-frozen RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen tasks [3], with ordering and clean-performance thresholds fixed before any perturbation results are observed. To avoid conflating perturbation-induced failures with insufficient nominal task competence, we apply predefined cleanperformance screen before perturbation evaluation. Each candidate is first evaluated over 10 clean rollouts; tasks with at most three successes are excluded as clean-floor cases, while the remaining candidates are extended to 20 rollouts. We retain all and only tasks achieving at least 12/20 clean successes, resulting in the four-task formal suite summarized in Table I. The complete screening results are provided in Appendix VI-A. The reported diagnostic milestone count is used only for stage-aware analysis and is distinct from official task-structure metadata, as described in Section IIID. TABLE I: Formal task suite used in RoboCasa-Shift. The official horizon, mobility label, and task-structure value are obtained from RoboCasa365 task metadata. Diagnostic milestones denote the task-specific semantic execution milestones used for stage-aware analysis and are not used as task-complexity labels. TABLE II: Validation of the counterfactual pairing protocol. Environment-side pairing is verified through the initial-state fingerprint. The policy-side comparison shows that uncontrolled inference randomness breaks repeatability, whereas sharing the episode-level policy seed restores consistent action sequences. Subgoal-Aware Failure Tracking Episode-level success indicates whether task is ultimately completed, but does not reveal how far the policy progresses before failure. We therefore represent each longhorizon task as an ordered sequence of semantic subgoals, = (g1, g2, . . . , gK), derived from the task logic and instruction. Each subgoal is associated with simulatorstate predicate that determines whether the corresponding task condition has been satisfied, such as an object reaching target receptacle or fixture entering required state. This provides simulator-grounded diagnostic of execution progress without requiring external stage annotations or model-predicted labels. this sequential We implement tracking procedure with StageTracker, which evaluates the predicate of the current subgoal at each rollout step. Once satisfied, the subgoal is marked as completed, its completion step is recorded, and the tracker advances to the next one. The tracker also B. Controlled Distribution Shifts RoboCasa-Shift considers four representative single-factor shifts that preserve the task objective while perturbing distinct sources of variation in household manipulation. Following robustness dimensions explored in recent VLA manipulation benchmarks [3], [4], [17], we evaluate illumination, third-person camera orientation, robot base initialization, and Gaussian blur. For L1L3, illumination scales simulator light intensity by α = {0.8, 0.6, 0.4}; camera orientation samples third-person yaw/pitch offsets within θmax = {2, 6, 10} while preserving the wrist view; base initialization uses σxy = {0.02, 0.05, 0.10} and σψ = {2, 5, 10} for planar position and yaw; and Gaussian blur applies σ = {1, 2, 4} to the RGB observations used by the policy. Implementation details and severity calibration procedures are provided in Appendix VI-B. Severity levels are calibrated before formal evaluation through model-free rendering and reset-state validity checks and are frozen independently of policy success. For camera and base shifts, the same factor-specific random draw is reused across L1L3 for each base episode, so severity changes only the perturbation magnitude; illumination and blur are deterministic. The levels are ordinal within each factor, and equal level indices across different factors do not imply physically equivalent perturbation magnitudes. C. Counterfactual Paired Evaluation Protocol To isolate changes associated with distribution shift from the inherent variability of RoboCasa episodes, we adopt paired counterfactual evaluation protocol. For each base episode ei, we construct clean rollout Eclean and its perturbed counterpart Ep,s , where denotes the perturbation factor and its severity. The paired rollouts share the same task and instruction, scene and object configuration, initial simulator state, episode horizon, and policy. For stochastic policies, the same policy-side random seed is initialized for both rollouts in pair and is not reset at every action step. The target perturbation is therefore the only controlled difference between Eclean , enabling direct comparison under otherwise matched conditions. We separately validate environment-state identity and policy-side repeatability, with the results summarized in Table II. Implementation details and pairing integrity audits are provided in Appendix VI-C. and Ep,s Fig. 3: Overview of StageTracker. (a) long-horizon task is represented as an ordered sequence of semantic subgoals, each associated with simulator-state predicate. (b) During rollout, StageTracker evaluates the current predicate, records the completion step when it is first satisfied, and advances to the next subgoal. Completed subgoals are latched, allowing the tracker to report the deepest semantic progress reached and the first incomplete subgoal for failure localization. records the first incomplete subgoal. Completed subgoals are latched rather than re-evaluated later, so the resulting trajectory represents the deepest semantic milestone reached during execution rather than the set of conditions satisfied at the terminal state. StageTracker therefore complements, rather than replaces, RoboCasas official task-success criterion by distinguishing failed executions according to their semantic progress. The procedure is illustrated in Figure 3. Task-specific subgoal specifications and their validation are provided in Appendix VI-D. E. Stage-Aware Robustness Measures RoboCasas official task-success criterion remains the primary end-to-end outcome, while StageTracker provides complementary measures of execution depth. For task with ordered subgoals, let mi denote how many are sequentially completed in episode i. We define the normalized subgoal progress as Progressi = , (1) mi which measures the deepest normalized semantic milestone reached during execution. At the task level, for evaluated episodes, the reach rate of gk is Rk = 1 (cid:88) i= I[mi k], (2) representing the fraction of rollouts that reach at least the k-th semantic milestone. To localize where execution terminates, we further define the first incomplete subgoal for episodes with mi < as fi = gmi+1. (3) The distribution of fi provides an operational stage-wise localization of failed executions according to the first unreached semantic milestone. It does not identify the causal instant at which failure is initiated. Episodes with mi = are not assigned fi, regardless of their final official tasksuccess label. These measures separate final task completion from the depth and location of execution failure. IV. EXPERIMENTS A. Experimental Setup Evaluation Configuration. We use the official GR00T N1.5 Composite-Seen checkpoint [18] as the primary policy, whose training scope matches the target Composite-Seen tasks used in our formal evaluation. All experiments are conducted on the RoboCasa365 target split [3] with OSMesa rendering. We evaluate the four clean-qualified tasks introduced in Section III-A, using 20 fixed base episodes per task. Each episode is evaluated under the clean condition and twelve shifted conditions spanning four perturbation factors and three severity levels, resulting in 20 13 = 260 rollouts per task and 1,040 formal rollouts in total. Each rollout uses the official task horizon, and all clean-perturbed executions follow the counterfactual pairing protocol in Section III-C. post-run integrity audit confirmed that all formal rollouts passed the base-state, policy-seed, renderer, and StageTracker consistency checks. Full model/runtime configurations and formal-evaluation integrity statistics are provided in Appendix VI-E. Evaluation Metrics and Statistical Analysis. We use RoboCasas official binary task success as the primary endto-end outcome and report success rate (SR) for each task and evaluation condition. For perturbation factor and severity level s, paired robustness degradation is measured as SRp,s = SRclean SRp,s, where positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Across the primary aggregate is the equal-weight macro tasks, average of task-level metrics rather than pooled estimate over episodes. Confidence intervals for paired degradation are obtained from 10,000 pair-level bootstrap resamples. Stage-aware analyses use the measures defined in Section IIIE. For failure localization, we consider only matched pairs in which the clean rollout succeeds and the corresponding perturbed rollout fails, focusing on failures emerging under the evaluated shift. Additional Policy Screening. We additionally screened two released RoboCasa-compatible VLA checkpoints, SmolVLA RoboCasa and π0 RoboCasa365 Human300, under the same interface and fixed-seed repeatability checks. Both passed these checks, but achieved only 1/40 and 2/40 clean successes, respectively, with no task satisfying the predefined competence gate. We therefore did not proceed to cross-model perturbation evaluation, and the formal perturbation results below are restricted to GR00T N1.5 on the clean-qualified task suite. Detailed clean-screening outcomes and policy compatibility assessments are provided in Appendix VI-I. Fig. 4: End-to-end robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Macro-averaged paired success-rate degradation SR is shown for the four distribution-shift factors, with each factor evaluated at three frozen severity levels (L1 L3). Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals obtained from paired bootstrap resampling. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor, and equal level indices across different factors do not imply physically equivalent perturbation magnitudes. Fig. 5: Task-level robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Each cell reports the paired success-rate degradation SR for one task and perturbation condition, computed from 20 matched episode pairs. Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition, while negative values indicate higher success rate under the shifted condition for the corresponding finite paired sample. The task-level breakdown reveals heterogeneous severity responses that can be obscured by macro aggregation. B. End-to-End Robustness under Controlled Distribution Shifts The evaluated policy does not exhibit universal relationship between perturbation severity and end-to-end robustness. Starting from clean macro success rate of 0.738, the four distribution-shift factors exhibit distinct severityresponse profiles. Moreover, the task-level breakdown shows that similar aggregate trends can arise from heterogeneous responses across individual tasks. Figure 4 summarizes the macro paired degradation, while Figure 5 shows the corresponding task-level variation. As shown in Figure 4, Gaussian blur exhibits the clearest and most consistent severity-linked degradation. The macro success rate decreases from 0.550 at L1 to 0.225 at L2 and reaches 0 at L3, corresponding to paired SR values of 0.188, 0.513, and 0.738, respectively. The paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero at all three severity levels. Robot base initialization also shows graded macrolevel response, with SR increasing from 0.075 at L1 to 0.150 at L2 and 0.263 at L3. The paired confidence intervals exclude zero at L2 and L3, but not at L1. The task-level breakdown in Figure 5 shows that these macro trends correspond to different degrees of cross-task consistency. Gaussian blur produces positive degradation across all four tasks, with task-level SR reaching 0.700.80 at L3. In contrast, the graded macro-level response to robot base initialization is not uniform across tasks. RinseSinkBasin increases from 0.25 to 0.40 and 0.55 across the three levels, whereas PreSoakPan changes from 0.05 to 0.20 and then returns to 0.05. Thus, graded macro-level response does not necessarily imply uniformly monotonic task-level response. Figure 4 shows qualitatively different response patterns for camera orientation and illumination. Camera orientation yields no macro degradation at L1, followed by SR values of 0.188 at L2 and 0.138 at L3, with the paired confidence intervals for the latter two levels excluding zero. The smaller degradation at L3 than at L2 shows that increasing calibrated severity does not necessarily translate into monotonically increasing policy degradation. Illumination produces only small net macro changes, with SR values of 0.012, 0.025, and 0.025, and all three paired confidence intervals include zero. Figure 5 further reveals heterogeneous task-level responses underlying these aggregate patterns. For camera orientation, PreSoakPan degrades progressively from 0.00 to 0.25 and 0.35, while the other tasks show smaller degradation at L3 than at L2 or changes in the opposite direction. Under illumination, task-level changes also occur in both directions, indicating that near-zero macro effect can coexist with heterogeneous task responses rather than uniformly unchanged behavior. End-to-end robustness therefore varies across perturbations and tasks, while observed severity responses are not uniformly monotonic. Complete conditionlevel numerical results are provided in Appendix VI-F. C. Counterfactual Sensitivity Beyond Aggregate Success Aggregate success-rate changes can mask substantial episode-level sensitivity to distribution shift. Under strict clean-perturbed pairing, each matched episode can be classified according to its clean and perturbed outcomes as success-to-success (S S), success-to-failure (S F), failure-to-success (F S), or failure-to-failure (F F), where the first and second symbols denote the clean and perturbed outcomes, respectively. The aggregate success-rate drop depends only on the net difference between the two outcome-changing transitions, SR = NSF NFS , (4) so opposing transition directions can partially or completely cancel at the aggregate level. Table III summarizes the paired outcome transitions across all twelve perturbation conditions. The three cases below highlight distinct relationships between aggregate degradation and pair-level outcome changes. Under camera orientation at L1, SR = 0.000 despite 8 of the 80 matched episodes changing outcome, as four and four transitions cancel exactly. Illumination at L2 shows similar mismatch, with SR = 0.025 despite 12 matched episodes changing outcome. In contrast, Gaussian blur at L3 produces 59 transitions and no transitions, yielding SR = 0.738. In this case, the pair-level outcome changes are strongly aligned with the aggregate degradation. These results distinguish net robustness degradation from counterfactual episode sensitivity. small SR does not imply that the underlying matched executions are insensitive to the shift, because and transitions can offset each other in the aggregate. Moreover, transitions should not be interpreted as evidence that perturbation improves robustness. They indicate only that the matched episode outcome changes under the shifted condition. Complete four-way outcome statistics and representative qualitative examples are provided in Appendices VI-G and VI-J respectively. D. Semantic Depth of Perturbation-Induced Failures Perturbation-induced failure episodes reach different semantic depths of task execution, depending on perturbation factor and severity. We restrict this analysis to strictly matched pairs. Across the twelve factor-severity conditions, we observe 247 condition-specific paired transitions in total. We characterize each cohort using normalized subgoal progress and the first incomplete semantic milestone, as summarized in Figure 6. Complete condition-level statistics and task-wise milestone distributions are provided in Appendix VI-H. Similar end-to-end degradation can nevertheless correspond to different semantic execution depths. Camera orientation at L2 and Gaussian blur at L1 produce the same macro degradation of SR = 0.188, yet exhibit different semantic execution-depth profiles. The camera-orientation cohort reaches mean normalized progress of 0.437, with 19.0% of failures occurring before the first tracked milestone. Under Gaussian blur, the corresponding mean progress is lower at 0.356, while the first-stage failure fraction increases TABLE III: Counterfactual outcome transitions across all perturbation conditions. Each condition contains 80 strictly matched cleanperturbed episode pairs. Changed denotes the number of pairs whose binary task outcome differs between the clean and perturbed executions. Thus, comparable changes in final task success can correspond to different semantic depths that end-to-end success alone cannot distinguish. Gaussian blur also exhibits the clearest severity-dependent shift in stage-aware execution depth. The number of events increases from 22 at L1 to 44 at L2 and 59 at L3, while the mean normalized subgoal progress decreases from 0.356 to 0.223 and finally to 0.000. Over the same severity range, the fraction of failures occurring before the first tracked milestone rises from 36.4% to 59.1% and then to 100%. At L3, all 59 perturbation-induced failures terminate before completing the first tracked semantic milestone. Stronger blur therefore affects not only how frequently cleansuccessful episodes fail under perturbation, but also how little semantic progress the resulting failure episodes achieve. The remaining perturbation factors exhibit weaker or less uniform localization patterns. For robot base initialization, mean normalized progress is 0.464, 0.465, and 0.340 from L1 to L3, while the first-stage failure fraction increases from 14.3% to 31.6% and 33.3%. This suggests tendency toward earlier failure under stronger base shifts, although the progression is not uniform across severity levels. Camera orientation produces failures across multiple execution depths, with mean progress decreasing modestly from 0.458 to 0.437 and 0.417, but without consistent monotonic change in the first-incomplete distribution. Illumination yields comparatively few events and does not show stable failurelocalization pattern over the evaluated severity range. The localization response therefore remains perturbation dependent rather than following universal severity trend. Representative matched replays in Figure 7 illustrate these differences, with perturbed executions terminating at different semantic depths under otherwise matched rollout conditions. Fig. 6: Stage-aware execution depth of perturbationinduced failures. Each marker summarizes strictly matched clean-success-to-perturbed-failure (S F) transitions under one perturbation factor and severity level. The vertical position indicates the mean normalized subgoal progress of the corresponding cohort, marker size represents the number of transition events, and marker color denotes the fraction of failures occurring before the first tracked semantic milestone. Fig. 7: Representative matched replays at different semantic failure depths. Each case compares strictly matched clean perturbed rollout pair that shares the same task instance, initial simulator state, episode metadata, and episode-level policy seed, while differing only in the target perturbation. The two rows show the clean and perturbed executions, respectively, and the columns present selected frames spanning the execution process. Checkmarks and crosses indicate whether the corresponding tracked semantic subgoals are completed, while the final annotation reports the official task outcome. These examples provide qualitative view of how perturbations can change execution depth and failure location, complementing the aggregate stage-aware statistics in Figure 6. E. Scope and Limitations The formal perturbation results are obtained with GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon RoboCasa tasks selected by the predefined clean-performance gate. Because no additional screened policy passed this gate, we do not claim crossmodel generalization. The four-task suite also does not support controlled claims across broader task structures or mobility settings. Our stage-aware diagnostics rely on audited simulator-state predicates rather than official perframe stage annotations and should therefore be interpreted as execution diagnostics rather than ground-truth stage labels. Finally, all evaluations are conducted in simulation, and whether the observed robustness patterns transfer to realrobot deployment remains to be validated. Extending the protocol to stronger policies, broader task coverage, and realrobot settings is an important direction for future work. V. CONCLUSION We presented RoboCasa-Shift, diagnostic robustness benchmark that combines matched clean-perturbed evaluation with simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics for long-horizon household manipulation. Our experiments show that robustness varies across perturbations and tasks, while aggregate success can mask substantial episode-level sensitivity. Similar end-to-end degradation can also arise from failures at different semantic depths, with stronger shifts in some conditions associated with earlier incomplete milestones. These findings motivate moving beyond endpointonly robustness reporting toward evaluation protocols that diagnose how distribution shifts affect task execution. REFERENCES [1] B. Zitkovich, T. Yu, S. Task Selection and Clean-Competence Screening The complete candidate-level clean-screening results are reported in Table IV. Although the 16-task candidate pool was frozen in advance, screening was executed in preregistered 12+4 schedule. The first 12 candidates yielded three clean-qualified tasks; because this was below the predefined minimum of four formal tasks, the remaining four pre-frozen candidates were activated. Among them, only WashLettuce passed the same clean-performance gate, producing the final four-task suite. B. Perturbation Implementation and Severity Calibration 1) Perturbation Implementation: The perturbations are implemented directly within the simulator or observation pipeline while keeping the underlying task configuration unchanged. Each perturbation modifies only the targeted factor, without altering task semantics, object placement, or language instructions. For illumination shifts, we modify the simulator lighting parameters by scaling the diffuse and ambient components. For camera-orientation shifts, we perturb the external camera pose while keeping wrist-mounted views unchanged. The camera transformation is applied before rendering, producing observation-level viewpoint changes without modifying the underlying scene geometry. For robot base initialization shifts, Gaussian offsets are sampled for the mobile base planar position and yaw orientation before rollout reset. The perturbation magnitude increases with severity while maintaining valid initial states. For Gaussian blur, the corruption is applied to RGB observations from all relevant camera streams using Gaussian filtering with increasing kernel scales. These implementations allow each factor to be evaluated independently while preserving paired cleanperturbed comparisons. 2) Severity Calibration: Before formal evaluation, we conducted model-free severity validity audit on the four formal tasks, using three fixed base episodes per task under the clean condition and twelve perturbation conditions. This yielded 156 reset/render records, which were checked for valid initialization, observation integrity, pre-perturbation state consistency, and the intended factor-specific changes. All 156 records passed the automatic validity checks, with no reported errors or pre-perturbation base-state fingerprint mismatches. Illumination and Gaussian blur showed the expected severity-dependent changes without monotonicity warnings, and manual contact-sheet inspection also passed. Counterfactual Pairing Validation 1) Pair Construction: Each perturbed rollout is generated from the corresponding clean episode configuration while preserving the matched task conditions and policyside stochasticity. The target perturbation is applied before execution, while the task objective and evaluation protocol remain unchanged. This construction controls episode-level variation and enables analysis of perturbation-induced outcome changes. 2) Pairing Integrity Audit: We validate pairing consistency from both environment and policy perspectives. For environment-side consistency, we compare simulator state fingerprints before perturbation injection between clean and perturbed executions. Matching fingerprints indicate that the two executions share the same pre-shift simulator configuration. For policy-side consistency, we restore the same policy checkpoint and random number generator state before paired execution. This controls stochastic variation introduced by policy sampling without assuming deterministic action generation. The final audit verifies that all paired executions satisfy the required consistency conditions before formal evaluation. The validation criteria are summarized in Table V. Additional Qualitative Counterfactual Examples Figure 10 presents two representative matched rollout pairs under camera orientation at L1, illustrating opposite directions of episode-level outcome changes. While StackBowlsCabinet exhibits clean-success-to-perturbed-failure transition, PreSoakPan shows the reverse transition. These examples complement the paired transition statistics in Section IV-C by providing qualitative view of outcome changes that can offset each other in aggregate success-rate measurements. additional evaluation, we also screened SmolVLA on separately frozen 24-task pool comprising 12 mobile and 12 non-mobile tasks. This screening contained 240 effective clean episodes, including 20 records reused from the initial clean screening on the frozen four-task evaluation suite. Only OpenStandMixerHead and WashLettuce achieved one success each out of ten episodes, while the remaining 22 tasks recorded no successes. Consequently, none of the 24 tasks qualified for clean-screen extension or subsequent perturbation evaluation. Two other released policies were considered but did not enter clean screening due to interface compatibility constraints. The official GR00T N1.7 base checkpoint the required ROBOCASA PANDA OMRON did not support embodiment at the policy-interface gate. Cosmos Policy, meanwhile, uses an arm-only action interface and its released RoboCasa task suite has no overlap with the four tasks used in our formal evaluation, preventing evaluation under the existing protocol without additional, unvalidated interface adaptations. Under the frozen evaluation protocol, none of the additional candidate policies progressed to perturbation evaluation. These screening outcomes establish the limits of the available policy-task coverage and should not be interpreted as cross-model robustness comparison or performance ranking. Columns show selected frames from the initial, intermediate, and final stages of execution, with the final outcomes determined by RoboCasas official task-success criterion. These examples illustrate opposite episode-level outcome changes under the same perturbation condition, despite zero aggregate success-rate degradation at L1.
